newsitem.title: UK: FOCUS-Lloyds TSB in board, insurance moves.
newsitem.headline: FOCUS-Lloyds TSB in board, insurance moves.

text.p: Lloyds TSB Group, Britain's largest retail financial services company, on Friday ended months of speculation over the future of its chief executive Brian Pitman by making him chairman and elevating his deputy.

The company named former TSB chief executive Peter Ellwood, to the top job in a move which was warmly greeted by banking analysts who had hoped for an internal appointment which would help continue the bank's recent good results record.
Lloyds TSB said its current chairman Robin Ibbs will retire in February when the changes take effect.
Lloyds TSB followed the news of its board changes by also ending speculation over its 62.6 percent-owned Lloyds Abbey Life insurance unit which is seperately quoted on the stock exchange.
It said it will pay 635p per share to buy-out the minority shareholding in the company in a shares and cash deal amounting to some 1.66 billion pounds ($2.6 billion).
"They have neatly solved the problem of retaining the bank's strategic direction," said Morgan Stanley's banking analyst Nick Collier of the board changes.

John Aitken, banking analyst at UBS, said one important aspect of the changes was that Ellwood was known to share Pitman's vision of Lloyds TSB's future. "Ellwood doesn't have to be persuaded of the strategy and that's important," said Aitken. "He has the same mind-set as Pitman."
Pitman, who is also the current president of the British Bankers' Association, is generally regarded as London's leading commercial banker.
The straight-talking and highly respected Pitman, 64, has been at Lloyds since 1952, sitting in the top job since 1983 and stewarding the bank to its current place as Britain's most profitable.

In the recent round of half-year figures, Lloyds TSB got the best reception of all the British banks notching up a startling 31 percent return on equity with the major cost savings from Lloyds' 1995 merger with TSB still to come.
It raised pre-tax profit by 12 percent to 1.14 billion pounds with one analyst commenting, "The results are so good, it's obscene."

Analysts were equally enthusiastic about Lloyds TSB's buy-out of the minority in Lloyds Abbey. In July, the life insurance unit posted a 28 pct jump in first half pre-tax profits to 259 million pounds -- well above market forecasts.

"It's a fine move," said Aitken at UBS. "Lloyds TSB is much better diversified in financial services -- insurance and pensions -- than the other British banks and they are now making a play for a strategically important share of that market."
Analysts said the move would be marginally earnings enhancing for Lloyds TSB this year and that the price paid looked fair.
"The market seems a bit disappointed but it's beyond me why anybody expected Lloyds TSB to pay a richer price for a company it already controls," Aitken said.
At 1230 GMT, Lloyds Abbey shares were 37p higher at 629p while Lloyds TSB dipped 8p to 382. ($1=.6439 Pound)
